For researchers

Sources & method

Recording provenance, the evidence behind a claim, and the difference between a written bar and a measured time.

MethodRecordingsDossiersScoresDownloadsCitation

How claims are labelled

Evidence belongs to each field

Documented
Stated in a cited source. This identifies the source’s claim; it does not guarantee that the source is right.
Inferred
Estimated from the evidence, not explicitly documented. The note gives the reasoning.
Disputed
Sources disagree. The dossier retains the alternatives and their sources.
Unknown
Not established from the sources consulted. An upload date is not a session date; an uploader is not necessarily a performer or transfer engineer.
Not applicable
The field does not apply. This is not a substitute for ‘unknown’.

What a cue time means

score-aligned
A written bar is matched to its performed occurrence in this recording. Repeats are counted separately.
score-proportion
Placement estimated from the score’s proportions. Tempo changes and pauses can move the event away from the estimated time.
audio-feature
A measured feature of this recording, such as a silence or a level change, locates the event. It does not by itself identify a chord or instrument.
documented
A fact from a cited source; it need not identify an audible event at that second.
general
A description of the surrounding stretch, not a claim about one instant.

Provisional alignment

A machine has matched score events to the recording; a named listener has not yet checked the published alignment against the score. A provisional bar time is an estimate, not an exact onset. ‘Reviewed’ records a listening check, with its scope and reviewer in the score data. Cue precision distinguishes a moment (about ±2 seconds) from a passage; neither label removes uncertainty in the underlying alignment.

Rights statements report the sources and their qualifications, not worldwide legal clearance. The composition, edition, performance, recording and digital transfer can have different rights.

Johann Sebastian Bach · Brandenburg Concerto No. 5, BWV 1050 · II. Affettuoso

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Advent Chamber Orchestra (ensemble), Roxana Pavel Goldstein (violin), Constance Schoepflin (flute), Matthew Ganong (harpsichord) Documented

The upstream programme confirms all three soloists. In the Affettuoso file’s Author field Goldstein is accidentally repeated as harpsichordist; its Description and the upstream programme both name Ganong. No conductor is credited. The slow movement uses only the three soloists.

Johann Sebastian Bach · St Matthew Passion, BWV 244 · No. 47. Erbarme dich, mein Gott

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Hertha Töpper (alto), Otto Büchner (solo violin), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor) Documented

The booklet lists Hertha Töpper for the alto arias and Otto Büchner as the violinist. The label of the LP side that carries Nos. 42–53 credits both and does not assign Büchner to a single number; his identification as this aria’s solo violinist rests on that label and on the booklet naming no other violinist. The booklet also names continuo players for the whole Passion (organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl, whom Discogs also lists on continuo cello); which of them play in this aria is not stated, so they are not listed here.

[3] [6] [5]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

The performing edition is not identified. The booklet numbers the aria 47 (the Bach-Gesellschaft and BWV numbering) while the Internet Archive and retail track titles number it 39 (the New Bach Edition). The file contains the aria alone: the preceding chorus and recitative ‘Wahrlich, du bist auch einer von denen — Da hub er an’ (booklet No. 46) is the previous track and the chorale ‘Bin ich gleich von dir gewichen’ is the next. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736.

[3] [2]
Recorded
23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August) Documented

The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958. Which session produced this aria is not stated.

Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.

[1] [2] [4]
Composition rights

IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.

[8]
Recording rights
territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959). Documented

Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

Johann Sebastian Bach · St Matthew Passion, BWV 244 · No. 1. Kommt, ihr Töchter, helft mir klagen

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Münchener Bach-Chor (chorus (Chorus I and II)), Münchener Chorknaben (boys’ choir, ripieno soprano (chorale ‘O Lamm Gottes, unschuldig’)), Münchener Bach-Orchester (orchestra), Karl Richter (conductor) Documented

The booklet track list gives the chorale to the Knabenchor. The booklet also names instrumental soloists for the whole Passion (flutes Walther Theurer and Wolfgang Haag; oboes Edgar Shann and Kurt Hausmann; organ Ekkehard Tietze and Hedwig Bilgram; double bass Franz Ortner; bassoon Karl Kolbinger; viola da gamba Oswald Uhl), and Fritz Rothschuh as chorus master. Their assignment to this number is not stated, so they are not listed as performers of it.

[3] [6] [5]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

The performing edition is not identified. The booklet gives the composition as Leipzig 1729 or earlier, revised 1736, and cites the autograph score Mus. ms. Bach P 25 and the parts St 110. The booklet and the Bach-Gesellschaft score number this chorus No. 1; the New Bach Edition also numbers it 1.

[3] [2]
Recorded
23 June – 21 August 1958 (sessions 23 June–6 July, 11–12 August and 21 August) Documented

The Archiv Produktion LP labels print the recording dates as 6/23–7/6, 8/11–12 and 21/1958; the retail page gives 23 June–6 July, 11–12 and 21 August 1958; the booklet essay gives 22 sessions between 23 June and 21 August 1958 and its credit line gives 6–8/1958. Which session produced No. 1 is not stated.

[6] [4] [3]
Place
Herkulessaal, Munich Documented

The booklet credit reads ‘München, Herkules-Saal’.

[3] [4]
Label
Archiv Produktion (Deutsche Grammophon Gesellschaft, History of Music Division) Documented

The labels read ‘Archive Production — History of Music Division Deutsche Grammophon Ges.’ and ‘Stereo’.

[6] [5]
Catalogue
SAPM 198 009/012 (first stereo edition, four LPs); the scanned export pressing carries ARC 73 125–73 128 / SAPM 198 625–628 Documented

First release year is disputed in the sources: the booklet and Wikipedia say 1959 (the booklet reads ‘LPs released/veröffentlicht/paru 1959’ and prints ℗ 1959 Deutsche Grammophon); Discogs and the Internet Archive LP catalogue give 1958, which is the recording year. Both dates precede 1963. The digital file used here is a later remaster, not the LP.

[5] [7] [6]
Matrix, take, sides
First stereo edition: first programme side of the set (Discogs side A), first track (9:50 on the LP); matrix and take numbers not read Documented

The side and position come from the Discogs tracklist only, whose first edition is automatically coupled, so the programme side is not the physical side of a particular LP. No run-out inscription was seen, so matrix and take are unknown.

[5]
Transfer
Unknown Unknown

No remastering engineer or studio is credited in the item metadata or the booklet. The booklet’s © 2001 Deutsche Grammophon notice and the retail page’s ‘Digitally remastered’ line show only that commercial digital releases exist. The upload is a private Internet Archive upload in the hifidelity collection.

[1] [4]
Transfer date
Unknown Unknown

No transfer date is established. The Internet Archive item was created on 16 February 2026; that upload date is not a transfer date.

Processing
24-bit/192 kHz FLAC (item description ‘1959 [FLAC 24-192]’), digitally remastered according to the retail page; streamed here through the Internet Archive’s VBR MP3 derivative. Inferred, not documented

The item’s track titles and durations (9:49 for this track) match the retail page’s 2016 hi-res listing, so the file is probably that release, but the item names no source. No speed correction, noise reduction or restoration settings are stated.

[1] [2] [4]
Composition rights
Bach’s composition (d. 1750) and the Bach-Gesellschaft edition used for the orchestra view (Breitkopf & Härtel, 1854) are public domain. Documented

IMSLP catalogues the Bach-Gesellschaft volume as Public Domain. This does not clear the sound recording, the later remaster or the booklet’s prose.

[8]
Recording rights
territorial — European recording-rights expiry; first publication documented before 1963 (Archiv Produktion stereo LP edition, 1958 or 1959). Documented

Programme rule 3. The recording was made in June–August 1958 and first issued on four stereo LPs; the booklet states 1959 and quotes a critic’s review of the four LPs from May 1959. Whether the first issue fell in 1958 or 1959, a recording published by 1959 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term (to the end of 2009) before the extension that applied from 1 November 2013. This is territorial, not a licence: the Internet Archive item carries no licence URL and no Public Domain Mark. US status is not established and no US public-domain claim is made. The audio file is a later commercial digital remaster; this dossier relies on the first publication of the recording and does not separately clear any rights claimed in the remastering, which is a point for the integration lead.

Performers
Pittsburgh Symphony Orchestra (orchestra), Fritz Reiner (conductor) Documented

The Archive explicitly identifies Pittsburgh, 1946. Its stored AcoustID resolves to a Pittsburgh/Reiner recording, corroborating that attribution rather than merely comparing durations. This is not the Chicago Symphony/RCA recording of 22 October 1955. The fingerprint database is supplementary, community-maintained evidence, not a fresh comparison performed here.

[1] [2] [5] [6]
Work version
Orchestral version; Reiner’s corrected conducting score, with Bartók’s revised finale ending. Documented

Móricz identifies the performing source as Reiner’s tissue proof CR, corrected by Bartók, and explicitly associates the 1946 recording with the new ending. The 1946 printed score is consulted for broad orchestration, not represented as Reiner’s exact performing copy; minor textual differences are not timed here. The Archive description mistakenly gives BB 127, which belongs to Piano Concerto No. 3.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: first lawful publication in 1948, before 1963. Documented

Móricz’s source RecR states first released in 1948; the Columbia discography identifies MM-793 and its 22 November 1948 issue. A contemporary March 1949 review independently establishes that the recording was commercially available as Columbia set 793 and ML-4102. This is a publication basis anywhere, not an assumption from the 1946 session. Its former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. The Archive’s legacy public-domain URL alone is not relied upon; it is an uploader declaration, not proof of the performers’ release.

Op. 131 dates from 1826 and was published after Beethoven’s death in 1827. IMSLP identifies the consulted engraving as the 1863 collected edition, plate B.50, and marks it Public Domain. This is not clearance of any unidentified later performing edition.

[9] [8] [10] [13]
Recording rights
United States public-domain basis: first published in 1924, before the project’s 1926 cutoff. Documented

The transfer author expressly dates Columbia L1581–L1585 and US 67021-D–67025-D/Set 6 to November 1924; DAHR corroborates their identity with the 1924 masters, not independently the November publication month. Under the Copyright Office’s stated 95-plus-5-year term for recordings first published in 1923–1946, a 1924 publication has exhausted that term. The Archive metadata supplies no separate Creative Commons recording licence. Admission rests on the historical recording’s US term, not Beethoven’s death, the upload date, an uploader licence or a blanket worldwide clearance. No separate restoration rights claim was identified in the consulted item.

Performers

The two photographed disc labels explicitly name all four players and their instruments. They do not label the violin chairs first and second; the dossier does not expand their order into a chair attribution.

[1] [3]
Work version
Original quartet scoring; movement III. The Archive’s combined III–IV designation is disputed. Disputed: sources disagree

The exact selected 1092.62-second MP3 is retained without truncation or substitution. Its analysed structure supports the five alternating spans of III, at approximately 0, 214, 340, 558 and 686 seconds, followed by slow music through the endpoint. The required report does not establish an A-major march or the IV–V link. Supplementary upper-band inspection finds an F-centred ending; verifier VerH independently checked the selected file’s final37.6s against the score and also found the F ending of III, not IV’s dominant recitative. These are score/audio-feature correspondences, not an aural or complete bar-aligned certification. No IV boundary or IV listening prose is invented. Performing edition, cuts, repeat observance and the completeness of the final played release remain unestablished.

  • III–IV combined, as asserted by the Archive filename and catalogue metadata
  • III only, supported by the selected file’s five-span design and independently checked F-centred endpoint

Recording rights
Territorial EU public-domain basis only: the recording was published before 1963; US status is not established. Documented

The admitted basis is eu-published-before-1963, using the Archive’s 1952 catalogue date for this identified London LLP318 issue. The printed sleeve carries a 1951 copyright notice, corroborating an early-1950s package but not independently establishing the first publication year of the sound recording. A recording published by 1952 had exhausted the ordinary EU 50-year phonogram term before 1 November 2013; the 2011 extension applies to recordings still protected on that date. This is territorial, not a Creative Commons grant or worldwide clearance. The US 1947–1956 term is longer, and no US public-domain claim is made. The Archive item supplies no separate recording licence; availability online and Beethoven’s public-domain composition are not the admission basis.

Rule 3 — territorial EU public domain: original sound recording first published in 1934. Documented

The Public Domain Project release-set catalogue explicitly dates first release of HMV DB 2211–2217 to 1934. Bloesch identifies the Appassionata issue as DB 2215–2217, matrices 2B 6605–6610, establishing publication separately from the 11 April 1933 recording date. Under the programme’s territorial EU rule, the earlier 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established; no worldwide clearance is claimed. Archive’s Public Domain Mark is not an ownership release, and the Public Domain Project’s worldwide/US expiry table is not relied upon. No CC licence or independently established additional rights in an unidentified modern transfer are asserted.

Marcus Bosch”, and the Munich analysis page repeats the credit. The Commons page credits only “University of Music and Theatre Munich” as author. No roster of players is given.

[2] [3] [5] [1]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

Neither the Commons page, the IMSLP performance entry, the embedded tags nor the Munich analysis page names the edition performed (Gutmann 1885, Haas, Nowak or Cohrs). The 1885 first edition is cited only as a viewable public-domain score for the orchestration timeline. Whether the cymbal-and-triangle clash at the climax is played is not established from the sources; the audio analysis cannot decide it.

[1] [2] [5]
Recorded
2020 (credits) or 8 November 2021 (inferred from file names and a programme listing) Disputed: sources disagree

The credits (IMSLP: “Live recording at the University of Music and Theatre Munich 2020”; embedded date tag; Commons; Munich analysis page) give 2020. The IMSLP file names, however, carry the token 2021-11-08, and the Gasteig November 2021 programme lists a Hochschulsymphonieorchester München concert under Marcus Bosch with Bruckner’s Seventh at the Isarphilharmonie, 19:00, under Mo 08. That matching concert is an inferred association, not proof that the files were cut from it; neither date is promoted to a settled session date, and no day or month is documented in the credits.

Hochschulsymphonieorchester (Munich) (orchestra), Marcus Bosch (conductor) Documented

The IMSLP performance entry gives “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (Munich), Marcus Bosch (conductor)”, the MP3’s embedded artist tag reads “Hochschulsymphonieorchester (München), Ltg. Marcus Bosch”, and the Munich analysis page repeats the credit. The Commons page credits only “University of Music and Theatre Munich” as author. No roster of players is given.

[2] [3] [5] [1]
Work version
Unknown Unknown

Neither the Commons page, the IMSLP performance entry, the embedded tags nor the Munich analysis page names the edition performed (Gutmann 1885, Haas, Nowak or Cohrs). The 1885 first edition is cited only as a viewable public-domain score for the orchestration timeline.

[1] [2] [5]
Recorded
2020 (credits) or 8 November 2021 (inferred from file names and a programme listing) Disputed: sources disagree

The credits (IMSLP: “Live recording at the University of Music and Theatre Munich 2020”; embedded date tag; Commons; Munich analysis page) give 2020. The IMSLP file names, however, carry the token 2021-11-08, and the Gasteig November 2021 programme lists a Hochschulsymphonieorchester München concert under Marcus Bosch with Bruckner’s Seventh at the Isarphilharmonie, 19:00, under Mo 08. That matching concert is an inferred association, not proof that the files were cut from it; neither date is promoted to a settled session date, and no day or month is documented in the credits.

  • 2020 (year only; credit on IMSLP, Commons, the embedded tags and the Munich analysis page)
  • 8 November 2021 (inferred from the IMSLP file-name token 2021-11-08 and the Gasteig programme listing)
[2] [3] [1] [5] [6]

University of Music and Theatre Munich (Hochschule für Musik und Theater München); the hall is not named in the credits Documented

IMSLP’s miscellaneous note and the embedded comment (“Live-Konzertmitschnitt der Hochschule für Musik und Theater München 2020”) name the institution as the place of the live recording, not a hall. The Gasteig programme lists a concert with the same forces at the Isarphilharmonie; whether the recording was made there is not established.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial: EU public domain on the pre-1963 original commercial acoustic Gramophone issue; US publication status is not established. Documented

The primary Symposium track-list scan identifies the historical commercial Gramophone disc 045578, matrix 1120m, in its 1916 chronology; the Archive instead prints 045678, and that catalogue discrepancy is preserved. The original acoustic commercial issue predates 1963, so the former European 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. The source rights year 1916 identifies that historical carrier chronology, not an independently established exact first-release date. The 1993 compilation is not represented as the original publication, and the uploader’s Public Domain Mark is not treated as a rights-owner release. No NC condition appears in the consulted source metadata.

Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach · Flute Concerto in G major, Wq 169 / H 445 · III. Presto

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Constance Schoepflin (flute), Advent Chamber Orchestra (orchestra) Documented

Both sources name the soloist and ensemble. The opened programme does not identify a conductor for this concerto or its continuo player. Credits for soloists in the adjacent Brandenburg concertos have not been transferred to this track. Exact string numbers, keyboard type, double-bass participation and tuning are unestablished.

[1] [3]
Work version
Flute version of the concerto; complete finale only Documented

Only movement III is hosted in this package. Set metadata records part 3 of 3, not possession of the preceding Allegro di molto and Largo. The 1755 date belongs to the original organ concerto Wq 34; the flute adaptation is later and cannot be assigned a precise year. The working manuscript is dated between 1755 and 1768 by Kuijken. The recording’s performing edition, any restored missing bar and the details of a cadenza are unestablished. The modern critical performing parts clarify the manuscript’s shorthand: flute participates in the opening and closing tutti, so a blank flute staff does not establish a rest. These parts are consulted as a reference, not attributed to the 2008 performance or claimed to be public domain. The score-derived orchestra display uses passage overviews rather than aligned entries; the cello desk represents written basso, not a verified allocation of bass instruments.

[1]
Recording rights
Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov-Military-Air Force (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov-Military-Air Force to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105(a), official US Government works are not protected by US copyright. This is rule 1’s recording-specific public-domain release route, not rule 2’s publication-date route; it does not establish worldwide public-domain status.

Edward Elgar · Pomp and Circumstance, Op. 39 · March No. 1 in D

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Royal Albert Hall Orchestra (orchestra), Edward Elgar (conductor) Documented

The label explicitly says conducted by Sir Edward Elgar; the composer credit alone was not used to infer this role.

[2] [1] [5]
Work version
Orchestral version Documented

The Elgar Society identifies this as Elgar’s first complete recording of the march, distinguishing it from the severely cut 1914 acoustic version. Complete does not establish that every written repeat was taken. The precise performing edition and organ participation are not established.

[2] [4]
Recorded
27 April 1926 Documented

Independently documented in the Elgar Society recording account and Naxos 8.111022 discography. Internet Archive’s date 1927 concerns the Victor issue, not the recording session. The identifier retains that issue year.

[4] [5]
Place
Queen’s Hall, London Documented

Venue is printed on the disc label; it is not inferred from the orchestra’s Royal Albert Hall name.

[2] [4] [5]
Label
Victrola (Victor Talking Machine Company) Documented

The label says Orthophonic Recording, identifying the electrical process.

[2]
Catalogue
9016-A Documented

Victor 9016 couples Marches Nos. 1 and 2; the January 1927 trade listing identifies the same performers.

[2] [3]
Matrix, take, sides
CR 336; Victor side 9016-A Documented

The specialist Naxos discography lists matrix CR 336-2 and original British issue HMV D 1102. The transferred pressing’s take suffix is not independently legible. Internet Archive’s matrix 9016A is the issue-side number, and its other ID CR331 is not silently adopted as the master number.

[5] [2] [1]
Transfer
George Blood, L.P.; Phoebe Pugh, transfer Documented

The item identifies the digitisation facility and user_transferred field; these are transfer credits, not original session personnel.

[1]
Transfer date
Unknown Unknown

The November 2023 upload does not establish the transfer date.

[1]
Processing
Digitised at 78 rpm; preferred 3.8 mil truncated-conical stylus transfer; equalised with turnover 250 and rolloff 0; MP3 derivative Documented

The original FLAC’s embedded comment identifies the selected stylus and equalisation. The site uses the supplied preferred MP3 without joining or changing the audio.

[1]
Composition rights
Elgar’s original 1901 march is public domain in ordinary life-plus-70 jurisdictions Inferred, not documented

Elgar died in 1934. This concerns the underlying composition, not an unidentified modern edition.

[5] [6] [8]
Recording rights
Territorial EU public-domain basis: Victor 9016 announced for publication on 28 January 1927 Documented

Rule 3. The Talking Machine World, 15 January 1927, p. 131, lists 9016 under the Victor list for 28 January, naming both marches and Elgar with the Royal Albert Hall Orchestra. This is publication evidence, not a session-date substitution; the British first issue may be earlier. Its 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected Great 78 item, original FLAC and label were checked; no NC licence or separate upstream digital recording is stated. [1] [5]
Recording rights
US-government sound recording: Commons explicitly applies PD-USGov-Military-Marines to the performance/recording Documented

Rule 1, recording-specific US-law basis under 17 USC §105, not worldwide CC clearance. Commons separates Performance/Recording from Composition and attributes the file to a Marine Band official-duty recording with an official .mil source. No CC-NC licence appears in the Commons record or the reviewed official source wording. Marine Band boilerplate says its institutionally distributed recordings ‘may not be distributed for private use and are not for sale’ because appropriated funds are used: this is the agency’s physical-distribution policy, not a non-commercial copyright licence on the government performance. Official web downloads are offered separately. Direct upstream retrieval returned HTTP 403 during this research; the official page’s indexed distribution wording and reader-accessible download instructions were examined, and the file’s recording-specific Commons declaration remains explicit. No claim of worldwide rights or a cleared private arrangement is made.

Work version
Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901) Inferred, not documented

The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Bernard Kruysen (baritone), Chorale Philippe Caillard (chorus), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ) Documented

Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording; Kruysen is the baritone soloist here (the sleeve credits “Bernard Kruysen, baryton”). Denis Thilliez has no part in this movement.

[1] [5] [6] [3]
Work version
Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901) Inferred, not documented

The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

The 1988 CD reissue notes “Recording: 08/1962”. Both candidate days fall in 1962; the rights assessment relies on that year only.

Gabriel Fauré · Requiem, Op. 48 · IV. Pie Jesu

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Denis Thilliez (boy soprano), Orchestre national de l’Opéra de Monte-Carlo (orchestra), Louis Frémaux (conductor), Henri Carol (organ) Documented

Commons lists Bernard Kruysen and Denis Thilliez among the artists of the complete recording. The sleeve credits “Denis Thilliez, soprano garçon” as the only soprano soloist, and the Pie Jesu is the Requiem’s only soprano solo, so his part here is inferred rather than stated. The chorus and baritone have no part in this movement.

[1] [5] [6] [3]
Work version
Full-orchestra version, as published by Éditions Hamelle (1901) Inferred, not documented

The sleeve credits “Editions Hamelle – Paris” and describes the version heard as the one with the more extended symphonic forces, which it says Fauré transcribed around 1899; Hamelle published the full-orchestra score in 1901. The sleeve names no editor or corrections, and the forces were not checked by ear against the score. Wikipedia notes that the 1900 autograph does not survive and that critics have asked who scored it, so authorship of the orchestration is not asserted here. The orchestra panel uses the Kalmus reprint of the Hamelle score.

George Frideric Handel · Water Music, Suite No. 2 in D, HWV 349 · I. Allegro

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor) Documented

Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. A harpsichord, strings with a double bass, a bassoon and a trumpet are visible in the Marine Band’s video frames; horns and oboes could not be identified there.

[1] [4] [2]
Work version
Performing edition not identified. The movement number (11 of the three suites), the 50 bars and the closing string-only Adagio match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text; no editor or continuo realisation is credited. Inferred, not documented

The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The numbering 11–15 for this suite follows the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) and IMSLP; other editions may agree. The recording plays the closing Adagio (bars 48–50, strings only): about six soft chord attacks, roughly three seconds apart, follow the last tutti chord, and the official video shows the violins playing at about 1:46–2:00. The stretch is identified from the score, the six level peaks and the video, not by listening; whether anything else is audible after the last chord has not been checked by ear.

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor) Documented

Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The wide shot in this video’s thumbnail shows a harpsichord at stage left, strings with a double bass and a bassoon; a trumpet is visible in the Hornpipe video, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each of the three passes is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 0:34, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

[1] [4] [2]
Work version
Performing edition not identified. The movement number (15 of the three suites) and the structure heard (a four-bar and an eight-bar strain, each repeated, the whole air played three times) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text and its instruction “This Air to be played 3 times over”; no editor or continuo realisation is credited. Inferred, not documented

The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The structure follows from the measured pauses and the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962), which prints 12 bars with repeat signs and the instruction on p. 53; IMSLP lists the movement as 12 bars played three times (36). The higher level of the third pass is a feature of this performance: the printed notes are the same for all three.

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Marine Chamber Orchestra, United States Marine Band (orchestra), Major Michelle A. Rakers (conductor) Documented

Commons gives the conductor as Major Michelle Rakers; the programme prints Major Michelle A. Rakers. No roster of individual players is published in the consulted sources. The video’s closing frames show the whole orchestra standing; the ensemble’s harpsichord, bassoon and trumpet are visible in the other movements’ videos, and no frame shows horns or oboes. Which sections play in each statement is not established: an independent look at the official video reports upper-string players resting at about 1:05, where the printed score gives them notes, so the recording is not assumed to follow the printed parts. No orchestra view is authored for this movement for that reason.

[1] [4] [2]
Work version
Performing edition not identified. The movement number (13 of the three suites) and the strains heard (a first strain of 8 bars and a second of 16, each played twice) match the Hallische Händel-Ausgabe text. The recording then plays all 24 bars once more without repeats, which that edition does not print; no editor or continuo realisation is credited. Inferred, not documented

The programme and Commons name the work and movement numbers but no edition. The Hallische Händel-Ausgabe (Redlich, 1962) prints 24 bars with a repeat sign after bar 8 and after bar 24 and no da capo; the second statement follows from the measured pauses (about 54 s for 24 bars at the first statement’s pace) and is a feature of this performance. Commons and the candidate list place this movement fifth in the suite; the edition numbers it third (13), and Arnold’s 1788 score prints it last, headed Coro.

Work version
Unknown Unknown

The performing edition and any editorial alterations are not identified in the recording sources.

[1]
Recorded
22 and 24 April 1929: the first side on 22 April, the second side on 24 April Documented

Young’s discography lists the first side (CVE-48983-2) with the 22 April 1929 session and the second side (CVE-48986-2) with a later recording date of 24 April 1929 for the published retaken side. DAHR’s list for 24 April 1929 includes CVE-48986 and Bolig gives take 2 for the second side. Commons’ 1 January 1929 is not a session day.

[4] [3] [6]
Place
Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts, United States Documented

Young heads the 22 April 1929 session “Symphony Hall, Boston, Massachusetts” and lists the 24 April retaken sides of the same symphony under that session; DAHR gives Symphony Hall, Boston for the Andante side CVE-48984. A separate place for the 24 April retakes is not given.

[4] [5]
Label
Victor Documented[2] [5]
Catalogue
Victor set M-55 (discs 7058–7060), released September 1929 Documented

Young lists the symphony as released 9/29 on M-55 (7058/60), with later AM-55, DM-55, HMV and LP issues. The upstream transfer also names set M-55 (Internet Archive description), and DAHR places the Andante on disc 7059. The disc number of this movement’s sides is not stated; the side order (sides 1–2 movement I, sides 3–4 the Andante, sides 5–6 the Menuetto and Finale) suggests 7058 for movement I and 7060 for the Menuetto and Finale, but that allocation is inferred.

[4] [2] [5]
Matrix, take, sides
Side 1: CVE-48983, take 2 (22 April 1929); side 2: CVE-48986, take 2 (24 April 1929) Documented

Young gives CVE-48983-2 and CVE-48986-2 as the issued takes of the first movement’s two sides. Bolig independently gives CVE-48986 take 2 for part 2. The DAHR matrix pages could not be opened on 17 October 2026 (503 error). No run-out inspection has been made of the digital surrogate.

[4] [6] [3]
Transfer
Bob Varney — transfer from original Victor 78s Documented[2]
Transfer date
Unknown Unknown

No transfer date is identified. The Internet Archive item was uploaded in December 2008, which is an upload date.

[1] [2]
Processing
Transfer from the original Victor 78 rpm set M-55 into one 20:48 file, from which the four movements were extracted as separate Commons files. Documented

The file lengths of the four Commons movements sum to the length of the Internet Archive file within about a second. The extraction procedure, stylus, playback curve, side-join locations and noise treatment are not documented.

Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

Commons applies PD-EU-audio to the Koussevitzky/Boston recording attributed to 1929, and the Internet Archive item carries a Creative Commons public-domain licence URL, not treated here as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The programme’s pre-1963 European rule applies because the 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension; Young gives the release as September 1929, which supports first publication well before 1963. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US status is not established.

Composition rights
Public-domain original composition, as asserted by Commons. Documented

The Commons description says the symphony was published before 1926; the composition is tagged PD-old-100-1923. The text comes from the Arnim and Brentano anthology Des Knaben Wunderhorn. This does not license a later edition, arrangement or recording.

[1]
Recording rights
Public-domain release attributed to Musopen, under a separate “Recording” licence line. Documented

The Commons page gives the recording its own licence, PD-author naming Musopen, separate from the composition tag; Musopen’s upload terms require uploaders to warrant that content is in the public domain. This records the source’s release, not an independent worldwide legal clearance, and the unidentified original recording cannot be checked.

Recording rights
Territorial EU public-domain basis: Columbia L 1798 was published no later than 3 March 1928 Documented

Rule 3. The Wanganui Chronicle’s dated review names L 1798, Mengelberg, the Concertgebouw Orchestra and the Adagietto, establishing publication independently of the May 1926 session. The exact first-release date remains unknown; source.rights.published 1928 is a documented upper bound. The recording’s 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. US status is not established. The selected item’s complete metadata, original-FLAC provenance and disc images disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial licence or separate upstream digital source. No licence is inferred from Mahler’s composition rights.

The item credits Kerstin Thorborg (alto), Carl Martin Öhmann (tenor) and Carl Schuricht (conductor) for the whole concert, and names the singer on each track; Carl Martin Öhmann does not sing in this song. The Mahler Foundation’s discography lists the same three with the Royal Concertgebouw Orchestra, Amsterdam. The orchestra was not yet styled “Royal” in 1939.

Processing
Internet Archive derivatives of a WAV original: this file is a variable-bit-rate MP3 (170 kbps); FLAC and spectrogram derivatives of the same WAV are also listed. Documented

The item description calls it “a good recording”. It does not describe noise reduction, speed correction or equalisation. The Internet Archive item also carries a separate 15-second clip (track 07, “Zwischenruf 6. Satz at 19 min 30 sec (3x)”) in which the uploader isolated an audience interjection that he places at about 19 min 30 s of this movement; the clip is not part of this recording and the words shouted are the uploader’s uncertain hearing.

Recording rights
Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established. Inferred, not documented

Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

[1]
Composition rights
Music by Gustav Mahler (died 1911); words adapted by Mahler from Hans Bethge’s Die chinesische Flöte (Bethge died 1946), itself a paraphrase of Tang-dynasty poems by way of French and German translations. The 1912 first edition is hosted on IMSLP as public domain. Inferred, not documented

A term calculation (life plus 70 years; Bethge’s text has been free in life-plus-70 jurisdictions since 2017), not a clearance of every edition or translation.

[11] [8] [12] [3] [4] [5]
Recording rights
Treated as public domain in the European Union (territorial): a live broadcast of 5 October 1939 whose related rights, on the sources consulted, had expired before the extended terms applied on 1 November 2013. United States status is not established. Inferred, not documented

Before the 2011 extension, Directive 2006/116/EC gave performers and phonogram producers 50-year terms. For a performance of 1939 the performer’s term ran 50 years from the performance, to 1989, unless a fixation of it in a phonogram was lawfully published or lawfully communicated to the public within that period, which would have started a longer term from that event. The live radio broadcast was a communication of the performance, not of a phonogram fixation, and the sources consulted document no earlier publication of the acetate fixation; the date of its first issue on disc is not given in them, so this is an inference, not a clearance. Directive 2011/77/EU lengthened terms to 70 years only for rights still protected on 1 November 2013 (Article 10(5)), so rights that had already expired were not revived. The item carries a Public Domain Mark 1.0 licence URL, which is the uploader’s statement and not the basis used here.

Work version
Unknown Unknown

The source identifies the orchestral song, but not its performing edition or editorial alterations. The listening notes use the low-voice orchestral score, C. F. Kahnt plate 4460, for passage-level scoring; they do not claim this exact printed edition was on the performers’ desks. In this transfer, songs IV–V have late pitch-class profiles about a semitone above the written score and the Fischer-Dieskau transfer. The cause—speed, transposition or other processing—has not been established. No tuning correction or numerical tempo comparison is asserted.

Gustav Mahler · Rückert-Lieder · Ich bin der Welt abhanden gekommen — concert-band arrangement

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Susan Kavinski (soprano (Chief Musician)), Richard Reed (English horn (Chief Musician)), United States Navy Concert Band (ensemble) Documented

As stated in the Commons description. No conductor is named in the consulted sources.

[1]
Work version
Arrangement for soprano, English horn solo and concert band; arranger not identified Inferred, not documented

Commons names the Navy Concert Band, a soprano and an English horn but does not name an arranger or edition. Mahler wrote the song for voice with piano or orchestra, so a band performance implies an arrangement. This recording’s chroma estimates read F major, whereas the first-edition orchestral score on IMSLP (22552) is notated in E♭ major; IMSLP lists the song in F major and notes transposed publications. The estimates suggest a possible pitch difference from that edition, but neither the arrangement’s key nor any transposition has been confirmed.

Performers
Soojin Han (violin (soloist)), Seokwon Hong (conductor), Hankyung Arte Philharmonic (orchestra) Documented

The video description on the YouTube channel named “한수진 Soojin Han” reads “Vn. Soojin Han / Cond. Seokwon Hong / Orch. Hankyung Arte Philharmonic”. The Commons file page names only the orchestra as author, linking the orchestra’s own site. That site’s news column reports a later concert (September 2026) played by the orchestra under a conductor named 홍석원 (Hong Seok-won, professor at Seoul National University), which supports the association but says nothing about the 2022 concert. No roster of players is given, and no second source for the soloist was opened.

Composition rights
Mozart’s concerto is public domain under the ordinary life-plus-70 term; Schnabel’s own cadenza is also beyond that term. Inferred, not documented

Mozart died in 1791; the consulted score derives from the 1878 Breitkopf edition. Schnabel died in 1951, giving an ordinary life-plus-70 expiry at the end of 2021 for his authorship. This is a territorial term calculation, not clearance of every modern edition or a claim about US cadenza publication history.

territorial — EU public-domain basis: first published in November 1937 on HMV DB3099–3102. Documented

The LSO discography documents publication before 1963, independently of the 1937 session date. The ordinary EU 50-year sound-recording term had expired before the 2013 extension, which applies to recordings still protected at that date. This package uses that territorial basis only. US public-domain status is not established: this is not a recording first published by 1925. The Archive uploader links http://creativecommons.org/licenses/publicdomain/, but that declaration does not independently establish authority to release the performers’ or producer’s rights worldwide. Lisa della Casa is the soprano soloist for this movement. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. The NMA labels the movement Süssmayr after Mozart’s Introitus and Kyrie. This is not an independently completed final movement in Mozart’s surviving manuscript. Süssmayr’s 1800 letter explains reuse of the Kyrie fugue; Constanze’s reported instruction from Mozart is testimony, not independent verification of a complete plan. File duration includes a retained live-recording tail after the estimated musical close.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · Requiem in D minor, K. 626 · III. Dies irae — Allegro assai

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor) Documented

This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

[1] [2] [3] [4]
Work version
Traditional Mozart–Süssmayr completion, Dies irae; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified. Inferred, not documented

Mozart left the vocal and bass framework and some instrumental indications; the traditional completed orchestration is used as the reference. The recording sources do not name a printed edition. The NMA preface quotes Walter’s policy of cutting some trombone doublings, but does not map it to this 1956 performance. The complete movement includes its orchestral postlude.

Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart · Requiem in D minor, K. 626 · VIII. Lacrimosa

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Wiener Staatsopernchor (chorus), Wiener Philharmoniker (orchestra), Franz Sauer (organ), Bruno Walter (conductor) Documented

This movement is for chorus, without a solo vocal part; the concert’s vocal solo quartet is not credited as singing here. Commons and Internet Archive name the Wiener Staatsopernchor; the festival catalogue uses Konzertvereinigung Wiener Staatsopernchor. The primary concert archive confirms Walter, the orchestra, all four concert soloists and Franz Sauer, but leaves its choir field blank. Ira Malaniuk, Anton Dermota and Cesare Siepi belong to the full concert cast, not to an invented solo entrance in this movement.

[1] [2] [3] [4]
Work version
Traditional Süssmayr completion of Mozart’s Lacrimosa; performing edition and Walter’s alterations unidentified. Inferred, not documented

Mozart’s surviving draft breaks off after bar 8. The conventional completion continues the movement and closes with the short Amen, rather than a later reconstructed Amen fugue. The NMA distinguishes Eybler’s separate attempted continuation from Süssmayr’s completed version. The upload does not identify its performing edition; no second-by-second authorship seam or session-specific trombone cut list is claimed.

Composition rights
Underlying Mozart–Süssmayr composition is out of copyright where the ordinary life-plus-70 term applies. Inferred, not documented

Mozart died in 1791 and Süssmayr in 1803; the traditional full score was published in 1800. This is a term-based assessment of the historical composition, not a worldwide clearance, a licence for a modern critical edition, or evidence about the sound recording.

[9] [10] [6] [13]
Recording rights
Rule 1 — territorial recording claim: Commons applies PD-EU-audio; upstream Internet Archive applies Public Domain Mark 1.0. Documented

The documented fact is the sources’ sound-recording rights assertion. PD-EU-audio is territorial: US status is not established, and no worldwide clearance is claimed. Public Domain Mark is not CC0 or a performer’s licence. The 1956 performance date does not prove first lawful publication or communication before 1963; that history is unestablished. The known 1996 Orfeo issue and 2018 uploads are not substituted for it. Admission therefore uses the explicit Commons PD-EU-audio route, not a calculated pre-1963-publication claim.

Hear this recording in the Hall

Performers
Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive and the Internet Archive) Disputed: sources disagree

Commons names no performer (“see Musopen for performance author information”) but files this page in categories for Neal O’Doan. The Free Music Archive album and the Internet Archive item credit the Skidmore College Orchestra; the audio of this file is orchestral, not a piano recording (editorial spectrogram inspection). The Musopen performer page itself was not opened. Conductor: unknown.

  • Skidmore College Orchestra (orchestra, as stated by the Free Music Archive album (15 tracks matching these Commons files by title and length) and the Internet Archive item for the first Promenade)
  • Neal O’Doan (pianist, implied only by the Commons categories “Audio files of classical music by Neal O’Doan” and “Nancy O’Doan” on this file page)
[4] [5] [1]
Work version
Orchestral performance; Ravel’s 1922 orchestration is the probable version but is not named by any source Inferred, not documented

Neither Commons, the Free Music Archive nor the Internet Archive names the orchestrator. The album’s four Promenades (none between “Samuel Goldenberg and Schmuÿle” and Limoges) match Ravel’s layout, and a 2015 Commons talk-page comment calls the recording Ravel’s orchestration of a rather poor Skidmore performance. The commenter gives no source. Instrument names in the listening notes follow Ravel’s scoring conditionally, as the introduction says; the audio report does not identify instruments.

Processing
Disc-to-DAT transfer, then digital remastering at BMG/RCA Studios, New York City; the Internet Archive derives its VBR MP3 from an uploaded WAV. Documented

The booklet says surface imperfections were reduced without radical removal of all surface noise. It gives no equalisation, pitch-correction, noise-reduction or editing settings, and none is inferred from the audio analysis. The booklet’s essay says the Edison engineer evidently placed the upright piano too far from the recording horns, so the sound is distant.

The Archive item’s Public Domain Mark is noted but not relied on. The 1992 booklet carries an all-rights-reserved reissue notice: no claim is made that its text, artwork or compilation is public domain, or that any new creative contribution to the mastering is cleared worldwide.

Performers
Sergei Rachmaninoff (piano) Documented[1] [3] [4]
Work version
Composer’s arrangement for piano (1911) of Franz Behr’s Scherzpolka Lachtäubchen, Op. 303, as played by him Documented

The printed title is Polka de W. R. (W. for Wassily, the composer’s father); the RCA set and the Archive file use V.R. Behr’s theme is transposed from F to A♭ with an added counter-melody and without Behr’s middle section. The score prints ossia alternatives, and the edition used by the composer for this recording is not identified.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

Commons supplies only composition-level PD-old-70; its description says November 1956, its filename says November 1959, and the dossier preserves an unexplained 1954 embedded date. All three attributions precede 1963. The opened Fricsay/RIAS commercial-carrier listing also documents French 1955 and German 1958 editions, but has not been matched to this transfer and does not settle its session. Usable under the programme’s pre-1963 European sound-recording rule; the former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US sound-recording status is not established. A recording date alone is not represented as an independently verified first-publication date.

Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

The Internet Archive item carries a CC0 licence URL declared by the uploader, which is not treated as authority to waive Victor’s rights. The pre-1963 European rule applies because the recording was made in 1927 and was on sale by January 1928 (a Victor advertisement in The Golden Book Magazine offers Records Nos. 6663-4-5), so the 50-year term expired before the 2013 extension; the exact first issue date is not established. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence. The recording was published after 1925, so a US public-domain basis is not established.

Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

Recording rights
Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105(a), official US Government works are not protected by US copyright. This is rule 1’s recording-specific public-domain release route, not rule 2’s publication-date route; it does not establish worldwide public-domain status. Commons separately specifies CC BY 3.0 for Pratt’s performance; the speculative PD-release suggestion is not needed.

Original sleeve and labels establish the displayed credit. Later Westminster reissue documentation and the publisher’s discography identify the orchestra as the Royal Philharmonic Orchestra. That cross-identification is not substituted silently for the original label credit; individual players and soloists are not established.

Work version
Unknown Unknown

The work and movement are identified, but the exact performing edition is not. The historical score supports broad orchestration and formal observations, not a claim of bar-exact agreement with Rodzinski’s materials. The movement is the entire supplied source track; no local audio edit is made. The set’s finale has a separately disclosed reported cut.

Composition rights
Not cleared as public domain in the EU or US; composition rights remain separate from the historic recording basis Inferred, not documented

Shostakovich died in 1975. The ordinary EU life-plus-70 calculation runs through 2045; this is not a global clearance or a statement of a US expiry date. IMSLP identifies the work as non-public-domain in the EU and US. The inspected score is territorially hosted as public domain in Taiwan and is cited, not republished. No composition licence is asserted.

[11] [14] [7]
Recording rights
Rule 3: territorial EU historic-recording basis; commercial circulation documented by December 1955, selected LP issue dated 1956 Documented

The original Westminster sleeve/labels and album metadata establish the selected 1956 WN 18001/XWN 18001 issue. A visually inspected High Fidelity review, December 1955, p. 80, already names this London orchestra, Rodzinski, his second recording of the Fifth and Westminster catalogue 18001; the review prints SWN 18001 and erroneously calls the symphony D major, so those details are not silently normalized. The publisher also lists Nixa WLP 20004 in 1955. First lawful publication anywhere before 1963 is the rule; no EU-first-release claim is required or made. source.rights.published 1956 remains a conservative upper bound tied to the selected physical issue, not a first-release date. Even using 1956, the ordinary 50-year recording term had expired before the 2013 extension. US sound-recording status is not established. Complete item metadata, original side-transfer provenance and scans disclose no Creative Commons non-commercial condition or separate upstream digital source. This is not a worldwide public-domain or composition-rights clearance.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established. Documented

A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — first lawful publication anywhere before 1963: London CS 6009, commercially published by 1958. Territorial EU sound-recording basis only; US sound-recording status is not established. Documented

A contemporary London/Pecar Electronics advertisement in the Grosse Pointe News, 6 November 1958, p. 7, pictures this Petrushka/Ansermet cover with catalogue CS 6009 under recordings NOW AVAILABLE. This directly establishes commercial availability in 1958; Archive’s 1958 carrier date and Decca’s ℗ 1958 attribution corroborate it. The rule concerns first lawful publication anywhere, not first EU publication; the US advertisement is therefore pertinent. A 1958 lawful publication exhausted the former 50-year EU performance/phonogram term by the end of 2008, before the 1 November 2013 protection threshold for the 70-year extension. The exact earliest market/day and any earlier issue are not established or required for this pre-1963 finding. No CC licence, worldwide public-domain claim, or US recording clearance is asserted.

Recording rights
Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov-Military-Air Force (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov-Military-Air Force to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. Under 17 U.S.C. § 105(a), official US Government works are not protected by US copyright. This is rule 1’s recording-specific public-domain release route, not rule 2’s publication-date route; it does not establish worldwide public-domain status.

Recording rights
Rule 3 — territorial: sound recording public domain in the European Union (pre-1963 publication basis). Documented

Commons describes first release in 1930; the Public Domain Project identifies Electrola EJ 423, order 6-0755, matrix CVE-48936, and tentatively dates first release to 1930. The 1929 session-day disagreement does not affect the pre-1963 release bound. The source’s worldwide expiry claim and its website’s CC BY-SA notice are not used as a sound-recording licence. Usable under the programme’s pre-1963 European sound-recording rule; the former 50-year term had expired before the 2013 extension. This is territorial, not a worldwide licence; US sound-recording status is not established. A recording date alone is not represented as an independently verified first-publication date.

  • Public-domain recording worldwide — claim made by the Public Domain Project and reproduced by Commons.
  • US pre-1972 sound-recording law provides a continuing term for a 1929/1930 first publication; no separate US permission is established.

Rule 1 — recording-specific public-domain release: PD-USGov-Military-Marines (US-law basis). Documented

Commons expressly applies PD-USGov-Military-Marines to the recording or official federal-government performance, not only to the composition. This is rule 1’s recording-specific public-domain release route, not rule 2’s publication-date route; it does not establish worldwide public-domain status.

Further reading

  • Timothy Day, A Century of Recorded Music: Listening to Musical History (Yale University Press, 2002 paperback).recording-history

    Examines how recording changed both listening and musical performance.

  • Mark Katz, Capturing Sound (University of California Press, 2010 edition).recording-history

    Studies the effects of recording technology on music-making and listening.

  • Robert Philip, Performing Music in the Age of Recording (Yale University Press, 2004).recording-history

    Studies recorded performance as evidence of changing musical practice, rather than treating recordings only as editions to collect.

Further reading

  • Clive Brown, Classical and Romantic Performing Practice, second edition (Oxford University Press, 2025).study

    Historical performing conventions in Classical and Romantic repertory; the linked scholarly review identifies the second edition.

  • John Butt, Playing with History: The Historical Approach to Musical Performance (Cambridge University Press, 2002).study

    Examines the intellectual claims of historically informed performance, including authenticity, intention, modernism and postmodernism.

  • Robert Philip, Performing Music in the Age of Recording (Yale University Press, 2004).recording-history

    Studies recorded performance as evidence of changing musical practice, rather than treating recordings only as editions to collect.
